name: Silures
note: The people of south-east Wales, who fought Rome from about AD 48 until their conquest in the mid 70s. Under Roman rule they formed a self-governing community with its centre at Venta Silurum (Caerwent), which lasted to the end of the Roman period. The name is first recorded by Roman writers in the 1st and 2nd centuries AD (Tacitus, Ptolemy); projecting the people back before the conquest is conjecture, and their territory had no known boundary.

name: Demetae
note: The people of south-west Wales, whose Roman-period centre was Moridunum (Carmarthen). Their name survived in the early medieval kingdom of Dyfed. The name is first recorded by Roman writers in the 1st and 2nd centuries AD (Tacitus, Ptolemy); projecting the people back before the conquest is conjecture, and their territory had no known boundary.

name: Ordovices
note: The people of central and north-west Wales. Agricola crushed their rising in AD 77 and founded Segontium afterwards. No Roman-period town or self-governing community is known for them. The name is first recorded by Roman writers in the 1st and 2nd centuries AD (Tacitus, Ptolemy); projecting the people back before the conquest is conjecture, and their territory had no known boundary. The end date is a placeholder: nothing is heard of them after Ptolemy (about AD 150).

name: Deceangli
note: The people of north-east Wales, attacked by the Roman governor Ostorius Scapula about AD 48. Lead ingots from Flintshire of the AD 70s are stamped with their name. The name is first recorded by Roman writers in the 1st and 2nd centuries AD (Tacitus, Ptolemy); projecting the people back before the conquest is conjecture, and their territory had no known boundary. The end date is a placeholder. No source was fetched for this entry; it rests on general knowledge of the standard literature.

name: Gwynedd
note: The kingdom of north-west Wales, with courts at Deganwy and Aberffraw. It became the strongest Welsh power under Rhodri Mawr (844-878), Gruffudd ap Cynan (died 1137), Owain Gwynedd and the two Llywelyns, and ended with Edward I’s conquest in 1282-3. The polygon is indicative for about 1200-1240 under Llywelyn ap Iorwerth: Gwynedd above and below the Conwy with Anglesey, Llŷn, Meirionnydd and Penllyn. The eastern part (the Perfeddwlad, between Conwy and Dee) changed hands repeatedly. The start date is conventional; the dynasty’s origin legend (Cunedda) is not history.

name: Powys
note: The kingdom of the central borderland. Its early extent reached further east, into what became Shropshire, before Mercian expansion and the building of Offa’s Dyke. Rhodri Mawr took it over in 855. It was divided for good after the death of Madog ap Maredudd in 1160. The polygon is indicative for about 1100-1160; it is not a surveyed boundary. The start date is conventional.

name: Powys Fadog
note: Northern Powys after the division of 1160, ruled from Castell Dinas Brân in the later 13th century; its princes founded Valle Crucis in 1201. It was broken up into marcher lordships (Bromfield and Yale, Chirk) after 1282-3. Only the Valle Crucis foundation is from a fetched source; the rest is general knowledge.

name: Powys Wenwynwyn
note: Southern Powys after the division of 1160, centred on Welshpool. Its ruler Gruffudd ap Gwenwynwyn submitted to Llywelyn ap Gruffudd in 1263, defected in 1274 and fought for Edward I; his heirs kept it as the marcher lordship of Powis.

name: Dyfed
note: The kingdom of south-west Wales, heir to the Roman-period Demetae, with a dynasty of partly Irish origin. Hywel Dda acquired it by marriage and joined it to Seisyllwg about 920 to form Deheubarth. The polygon is indicative for about 800. The start date is conventional.

name: Ceredigion
note: A small kingdom on Cardigan Bay between the Dyfi and the Teifi, by tradition founded by Ceredig. About 730 its king Seisyll is said to have annexed Ystrad Tywi, creating the larger kingdom later called Seisyllwg. The polygon follows the later county and is indicative. Dates are traditional. No source was fetched for this entry; it rests on general knowledge of the standard literature.

name: Seisyllwg
note: Ceredigion together with Ystrad Tywi (the Tywi valley). On the death of its king Gwgon in 872 it came under Rhodri Mawr; his grandson Hywel Dda joined it to Dyfed about 920 to form Deheubarth. The name ‘Seisyllwg’ appears only in later texts and some historians doubt it was used at the time; the start date is traditional.

name: Deheubarth
note: The kingdom of the south-west, formed about 920 when Hywel Dda united Dyfed and Seisyllwg. The Normans overran most of it after 1093; Rhys ap Gruffudd (the Lord Rhys) rebuilt it between 1155 and his death in 1197, after which it split among his descendants, who lost their last lands in 1277-87. The polygon is indicative for the Lord Rhys’s rule about 1170-1197: Ceredigion, Ystrad Tywi and parts of Dyfed, excluding the Norman lordships of Pembroke and Gower.

name: Glywysing (later Morgannwg)
note: The kingdom between the Tawe and the Usk. In the 10th century, united with Gwent under Morgan Hen (died 974), it came to be called Morgannwg, the origin of ‘Glamorgan’. The Norman Robert fitz Hamon conquered the lowlands about 1091-3. The polygon is indicative for about 950 and excludes Gwent. The start date is conventional. No source was fetched for this entry; it rests on general knowledge of the standard literature.

name: Gwent
note: The kingdom between the Usk and the Wye, named after Venta Silurum (Caerwent). It was at times joined with Glywysing. William fitz Osbern began its conquest from Chepstow after 1067. The polygon is indicative for about 1000. The start and end dates are approximate.

name: Brycheiniog
note: A small kingdom in the upper Usk valley with a dynasty claiming Irish descent. Its king built the Llangorse crannog about 890; a Mercian army destroyed it in 916. Bernard de Neufmarché conquered the kingdom in 1093 and it became the lordship of Brecon. The polygon is indicative for about 900. The start date is conventional; the conquest date is from general knowledge.

name: Lands of Rhodri Mawr
note: Rhodri became king of Gwynedd in 844, took Powys in 855 and Seisyllwg in 872, so that for a few years one king ruled most of Wales outside the south-east and Dyfed. He was killed fighting the English; the Dictionary of Welsh Biography gives 877, other reckonings 878. His sons divided the lands. No boundary is drawn because none is known.

name: Lands of Hywel Dda
note: Hywel held Seisyllwg from 920 and Dyfed by marriage, and on the death of Idwal Foel in 942 took Gwynedd (and with it Powys), ruling all Wales except Morgannwg and Gwent until his death in 950. The Welsh law-books are attributed to him, though no manuscript is earlier than the 13th century. His kingdom broke up at his death.

name: Kingdom of Gruffudd ap Llywelyn
note: King of Gwynedd and Powys from 1039, Gruffudd took Deheubarth in 1055 and Morgannwg soon after: the only king ever to rule the whole of Wales, with land east of Offa’s Dyke as well. Harold Godwinson’s campaign of 1063 broke his power and he was killed by his own men (5 August 1063 in the usual reckoning; the Dictionary of Welsh Biography’s revised article argues for 1064). The polygon is modern Wales, used as an indication; his holdings beyond the dyke are not drawn.

name: Principality of Wales (Llywelyn ap Gruffudd)
note: Llywelyn ap Gruffudd took the homage of the other Welsh lords in 1258 and styled himself Prince of Wales; Henry III recognised the title and the principality in the Treaty of Montgomery (1267). Edward I’s war of 1276-7 cut it back to Gwynedd west of the Conwy; Llywelyn was killed in December 1282 and his brother Dafydd captured in 1283. The polygon is a rough indication of the lands under Llywelyn’s lordship at the treaty in 1267: Gwynedd, both parts of Powys, Builth, Brecon, Gwerthrynion and the Welsh lords of Deheubarth. Its southern and eastern edges were contested and are not well defined.

name: Principality of Wales (royal counties of Anglesey, Caernarfon and Merioneth)
note: After the conquest the Statute of Rhuddlan (1284) annexed Llywelyn’s principality to the English crown and set up counties on the English model, governed from Caernarfon. From 1301 the principality was usually granted to the king’s eldest son. Flintshire, also created in 1284, was attached to Chester and is not drawn. The polygon is indicative: the three north-western shires as they stood from 1284. The Laws in Wales Act of 1535-6 ended the legal distinction between Principality and March.

name: Principality of Wales (royal counties of Cardigan and Carmarthen)
note: The southern part of the crown’s principality: the counties of Cardigan and Carmarthen, governed from Carmarthen and built up from royal lands held since the 1240s and the forfeited lands of the princes of Deheubarth (1277-87). The polygon is indicative for about 1300; medieval Carmarthenshire was smaller than the later county and its edges against the marcher lordships of Kidwelly, Llandovery and Emlyn are approximate. The make-up of these counties is from general knowledge.

name: March of Wales (marcher lordships)
note: The belt of some forty or more lordships along the border and across south Wales, conquered piecemeal by Norman lords from 1067 (Chepstow, Montgomery, Brecon, Glamorgan, Pembroke) and enlarged after 1282 with new lordships in the north-east (Denbigh, Ruthin, Bromfield and Yale, Chirk). Each lord held royal powers in his lordship and the king’s writ did not run there. The Laws in Wales Act of 1535-6 abolished these powers and divided the lordships among new and existing shires. No polygon is drawn: the March was not one territory, and its extent changed with every war.

name: Wales under Owain Glyndŵr
note: Owain Glyndŵr attacked Ruthin on 16 September 1400 and took the title Prince of Wales. After Bryn Glas (1402) and the capture of Aberystwyth and Harlech (1404) he controlled most of Wales, made a treaty with France and planned a parliament and an independent Welsh church. Defeats from 1405 and the loss of Aberystwyth and Harlech (1408-9) ended his rule; he still raided in 1410 and is not heard of after 1412. The end date is nominal: he never surrendered and probably died about 1415-16. No polygon is drawn because control shifted from year to year.

name: Wales (shired and united with England)
note: The Laws in Wales Acts of 1535-6 and 1542-3 united Wales with England, abolished the powers of the marcher lords, created the counties of Monmouth, Brecknock, Radnor, Montgomery and Denbigh beside the older ones, gave Wales members of Parliament and made English the language of the courts. The acts also fixed the boundary with England. The polygon is the modern outline of Wales, generalised; it includes Monmouthshire, which the 1542-3 act placed under the Westminster courts and whose status was long ambiguous. The fetched legislation.gov.uk pages confirm the two acts and their dates; the summary of their provisions is from general knowledge.

name: Cantiaci
note: People of Kent, with a centre at Canterbury. Named in Roman sources (Caesar, Tacitus, Ptolemy) and on coins or inscriptions; the label marks the heartland only, no boundary is known, and the name outlived the conquest as a Roman civitas. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

name: Trinovantes
note: People of Essex and south Suffolk; Caesar restored their king Mandubracius in 54 BCE. Named in Roman sources (Caesar, Tacitus, Ptolemy) and on coins or inscriptions; the label marks the heartland only, no boundary is known, and the name outlived the conquest as a Roman civitas. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

name: Catuvellauni
note: The dominant power north of the Thames under Tasciovanus and Cunobelin, with centres at Verlamion and, by conquest, Camulodunon. Named in Roman sources (Caesar, Tacitus, Ptolemy) and on coins or inscriptions; the label marks the heartland only, no boundary is known, and the name outlived the conquest as a Roman civitas. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

name: Iceni
note: People of Norfolk and north Suffolk, a client kingdom until Boudica's revolt of 60/61. Named in Roman sources (Caesar, Tacitus, Ptolemy) and on coins or inscriptions; the label marks the heartland only, no boundary is known, and the name outlived the conquest as a Roman civitas. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

name: Atrebates
note: A kingdom ruled by the heirs of Commius, centred on Calleva (Silchester). Named in Roman sources (Caesar, Tacitus, Ptolemy) and on coins or inscriptions; the label marks the heartland only, no boundary is known, and the name outlived the conquest as a Roman civitas. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

name: Regni
note: People of Sussex; the name's form (Regni or Regini) is uncertain and it may be a Roman creation for Togidubnus's client kingdom. Named in Roman sources (Caesar, Tacitus, Ptolemy) and on coins or inscriptions; the label marks the heartland only, no boundary is known, and the name outlived the conquest as a Roman civitas. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

name: Belgae
note: A civitas centred on Winchester; it may be a Roman administrative grouping rather than a pre-conquest people. Named in Roman sources (Caesar, Tacitus, Ptolemy) and on coins or inscriptions; the label marks the heartland only, no boundary is known, and the name outlived the conquest as a Roman civitas. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

name: Durotriges
note: People of Dorset and south Somerset, the builders of the last great hillforts. Named in Roman sources (Caesar, Tacitus, Ptolemy) and on coins or inscriptions; the label marks the heartland only, no boundary is known, and the name outlived the conquest as a Roman civitas. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

name: Dumnonii
note: People of Devon and Cornwall, later centred on Exeter. Named in Roman sources (Caesar, Tacitus, Ptolemy) and on coins or inscriptions; the label marks the heartland only, no boundary is known, and the name outlived the conquest as a Roman civitas. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

name: Dobunni
note: People of the Cotswolds and lower Severn, later centred on Cirencester. Named in Roman sources (Caesar, Tacitus, Ptolemy) and on coins or inscriptions; the label marks the heartland only, no boundary is known, and the name outlived the conquest as a Roman civitas. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

name: Corieltauvi
note: People of the east Midlands, later centred on Leicester; formerly read as 'Coritani'. Named in Roman sources (Caesar, Tacitus, Ptolemy) and on coins or inscriptions; the label marks the heartland only, no boundary is known, and the name outlived the conquest as a Roman civitas. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

name: Cornovii
note: People of Shropshire and Cheshire, later centred on Wroxeter. Named in Roman sources (Caesar, Tacitus, Ptolemy) and on coins or inscriptions; the label marks the heartland only, no boundary is known, and the name outlived the conquest as a Roman civitas.

name: Brigantes
note: A large confederation across the Pennines, ruled by Cartimandua as a client of Rome until about 69. Named in Roman sources (Caesar, Tacitus, Ptolemy) and on coins or inscriptions; the label marks the heartland only, no boundary is known, and the name outlived the conquest as a Roman civitas. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

name: Parisi
note: People of east Yorkshire, known for chariot burials. Named in Roman sources (Caesar, Tacitus, Ptolemy) and on coins or inscriptions; the label marks the heartland only, no boundary is known, and the name outlived the conquest as a Roman civitas. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

name: Carvetii
note: People of the Eden valley and Solway plain, attested only by 3rd-century inscriptions; probably a sub-group of the Brigantes before then. Named in Roman sources (Caesar, Tacitus, Ptolemy) and on coins or inscriptions; the label marks the heartland only, no boundary is known, and the name outlived the conquest as a Roman civitas. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

name: Votadini
note: People of Northumberland and Lothian, mostly beyond the northern edge of this map. Named in Roman sources (Caesar, Tacitus, Ptolemy) and on coins or inscriptions; the label marks the heartland only, no boundary is known, and the name outlived the conquest as a Roman civitas. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

name: Britannia
note: The single Roman province, governed by a consular legate. Its limit moved north by stages to Hadrian's Wall (from 122). No polygon: the area held changed decade by decade in the 1st century. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

name: Britannia Superior
note: The southern province after Severus split Britain; governed from London. The division is placed about 197 by one ancient account and as late as 213 by modern scholars. The line between the two provinces is not recorded. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

name: Britannia Inferior
note: The northern province, governed from York, which was a colonia by 237. Same dating caveat as Britannia Superior. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

name: Maxima Caesariensis
note: Usually placed in the south-east with London as capital. One of the four provinces of the Diocese of the Britains, created between 296 and about 312. Their names are certain; their boundaries and, for most, their capitals are not, and the label position is the common modern reconstruction only. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

name: Britannia Prima
note: Usually placed in the west, with Cirencester as capital on the evidence of one inscription. One of the four provinces of the Diocese of the Britains, created between 296 and about 312. Their names are certain; their boundaries and, for most, their capitals are not, and the label position is the common modern reconstruction only. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

name: Flavia Caesariensis
note: Usually placed in the east Midlands around Lincoln, though some would exchange it with Britannia Secunda. One of the four provinces of the Diocese of the Britains, created between 296 and about 312. Their names are certain; their boundaries and, for most, their capitals are not, and the label position is the common modern reconstruction only. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

name: Britannia Secunda
note: Usually placed in the north around York, though some would exchange it with Flavia Caesariensis. One of the four provinces of the Diocese of the Britains, created between 296 and about 312. Their names are certain; their boundaries and, for most, their capitals are not, and the label position is the common modern reconstruction only. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

name: Valentia
note: A fifth province named by Ammianus as restored by Count Theodosius in 369. Its location is unknown: around Carlisle (shown), around Chester, or between the Walls have all been argued. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

name: Kingdom of Kent
note: Traditionally founded about 455; its first securely attested king, Aethelberht, received Augustine in 597. Under Mercian control 764-825, then absorbed by Wessex. The polygon is the kingdom of about 600, roughly the later county. Frontiers were zones of shifting lordship, not lines. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

name: Kingdom of the South Saxons
note: Traditional foundation by Aelle in 477; converted by Wilfrid from 681; under Mercia 771-796, subject to Wessex from about 827 and fully absorbed in 860. The polygon is the kingdom of about 700, bounded inland by the Weald forest. Frontiers were zones of shifting lordship, not lines. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

name: Kingdom of the East Saxons
note: Founded in the 6th century (527 is a traditional and uncertain date). It ceded itself to Wessex in 825. The polygon is the kingdom of about 650, when it still included Middlesex, London and much of Hertfordshire; Mercia took those by the mid 8th century. Frontiers were zones of shifting lordship, not lines. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

name: Kingdom of the East Angles
note: Organised in the first half of the 6th century and ruled by the Wuffingas, of whom Raedwald (died about 624) was the most powerful. King Edmund was killed by the Danes in 869. The polygon is the kingdom of about 700: Norfolk and Suffolk, with the Fens as its western march. Frontiers were zones of shifting lordship, not lines. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

name: Danish kingdom of East Anglia
note: East Anglia under Danish kings, including Guthrum (baptised Aethelstan) from 880; it also held Essex. Submitted to Edward the Elder in 917-918. No polygon: its western limit is not known. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

name: Kingdom of the West Saxons
note: 519 is the legendary date of Cerdic; the historical kingdom grew from the Gewisse of the upper Thames in the 7th century. From 825 it also held Kent, Sussex, Surrey and Essex, and from about 886 Alfred styled himself king of the Anglo-Saxons. The polygon is the core kingdom of about 800, before those gains, with Devon included and Cornwall still British. Frontiers were zones of shifting lordship, not lines. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

name: Kingdom of the Mercians
note: Attested from the late 6th century and dominant south of the Humber under Penda (died 655), Aethelbald and Offa (757-796). The Danes took its eastern half in 877; the western half was ruled by Ealdorman Aethelred and Aethelflaed under West Saxon lordship until Edward the Elder annexed it in 918. The polygon is Mercia proper about 790 under Offa, including Lindsey, the Hwicce, Middlesex and London but not the client kingdoms of Kent, Sussex, Essex and East Anglia. Frontiers were zones of shifting lordship, not lines. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

name: Bernicia
note: The northern Anglian kingdom, centred on Bamburgh; 547 is the traditional date of Ida. It may have begun as a British kingdom. United with Deira for good by 654. Extent unknown. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

name: Deira
note: The southern Anglian kingdom between Humber and Tees, centred on the Yorkshire Wolds and York. Its last king was killed in 651 and it was ruled from Bernicia thereafter. The start date is nominal. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

name: Kingdom of the Northumbrians
note: Bernicia and Deira united. At its height it ran from the Humber and Mersey to the Firth of Forth; the polygon shows about 700 and is cut off at the northern edge of this map. York fell to the Great Army in 867. Frontiers were zones of shifting lordship, not lines. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

name: Lindsey
note: A small kingdom between the Humber and the Witham with its own king-list and bishop. It was fought over by Northumbria and Mercia in the 7th century and was Mercian for good by about 700. Both dates are nominal. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

name: Hwicce
note: A kingdom of the lower Severn and Cotswolds (roughly the later diocese of Worcester), a Mercian sub-kingdom from about 628; its rulers cease to be called kings about 780. The 577 start is the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle's and doubtful. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

name: Elmet
note: A British kingdom around Leeds, annexed by Edwin of Northumbria about 617. Start date nominal; extent unknown. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

name: Dumnonia
note: The British kingdom of the south-west. Wessex took Devon by the early 8th century; Cornwall kept kings until the 9th century and was brought under English rule between Egbert's victory at Hingston Down (838) and Aethelstan. Label placed in Cornwall; dates nominal. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

name: Kingdom of York
note: Scandinavian kingdom between Humber and Tees after the Great Army took York in 866/7. Taken by Aethelstan in 927, lost again, and ended when Eric Bloodaxe was driven out and killed in 954. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

name: Danelaw
note: Not a state but the part of England under Danish armies and law: East Anglia, the Five Boroughs (Lincoln, Stamford, Leicester, Nottingham, Derby) and York. The polygon shows about 890, with the Alfred-Guthrum treaty boundary (886-890) on the south-west running up the Lea to Bedford and then along Watling Street. Edward the Elder and Aethelflaed retook everything south of the Humber in the 910s; the term itself is first used in the 11th century. Frontiers were zones of shifting lordship, not lines. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

name: Kingdom of the English (England)
note: Aethelstan took York in 927 and was the first king to rule all the English. The polygon is the kingdom of about 1000: Cumbria was under Strathclyde until William II took Carlisle in 1092, Lothian had passed to the Scots, the Tweed border was fixed in practice only in the 12th-13th centuries (Berwick 1482), and Wales was annexed in law in 1536-42. Frontiers were zones of shifting lordship, not lines. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

name: Earldom of Wessex
note: Held by Godwin from about 1020 and by his son Harold from 1053 until he became king. One of the great earldoms through which Cnut and Edward the Confessor governed. Label only: earldoms were bundles of shires that were regrouped whenever an earl died or fell. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

name: Earldom of Mercia
note: Held by Eadric Streona, then by Leofric, Aelfgar and Edwin. End date approximate. One of the great earldoms through which Cnut and Edward the Confessor governed. Label only: earldoms were bundles of shires that were regrouped whenever an earl died or fell. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

name: Earldom of East Anglia
note: Held by Thorkell the Tall and later by Harold and Gyrth Godwinson; suppressed after the revolt of 1075. One of the great earldoms through which Cnut and Edward the Confessor governed. Label only: earldoms were bundles of shires that were regrouped whenever an earl died or fell. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

name: Earldom of Northumbria
note: After 954 the north was governed by earls appointed by the English kings, among them Siward and Tostig; the house of Bamburgh kept the land beyond the Tees for much of the time. Label only. The last English earl, Waltheof, fell in 1075-6 (from memory). Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

name: Earldom of Chester
note: Marcher earldom created by William I to contain north Wales; a palatinate, annexed to the Crown in 1237 (date from memory). Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

name: Earldom of Shrewsbury
note: Marcher earldom of Roger of Montgomery; forfeited by Robert of Belleme in 1102 (dates from memory). Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

name: Earldom of Hereford
note: Marcher earldom of William fitz Osbern; forfeited by his son after the revolt of 1075 (dates from memory). Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.
